transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-07-09 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lila Cho (Redwood SE), Damien Ortiz (Redwood SE), Jared Molina (Orion - Platform), Priya Narayan (Orion - Lead SRE), Evan Brooks (Orion - Security)

Summary: quick recap at top, but full transcript below. Note: auto-transcription has small errors (K V cache sometimes written K V cache, PrivateLink sometimes 'private link').

[00:00] Samir: hey everybody, thanks for carving time today. I think agenda is VPC egress, private connectivity, runtime impacts like KV cache and batching. we'll call out known hairpins.
[00:22] Jared: cool, yeah we wanted to understand the network patterns, especially because our regulatory folks want no public egress for PHI. so the question is, can Redwood Private run in our isolated subnets without hitting the internet for model serving?
[00:37] Lila: short answer yes, with caveats. you can either use PrivateLink to expose the inference API into your VPC, or you can deploy Redwood Private inside your VPC‍—in which case egress only needed for optional telemetry or to pull model artifacts. if telemetry is restricted, we support an airgap package.
[01:05] Priya: if we go PrivateLink, how do we handle egress for downloading container images or pulling checkpoints? our current plan is to use an internal artifact repo but some ops still rely on s3 endpoints.
[01:25] Damien: for model onboarding we recommend either a pre-staged S3 in the same region with VPC endpoint or scp transfer into the node. PrivateLink doesn't magically give you S3 access; it's about ingress to the service endpoints. so, commonly customers put a NAT gateway in a controlled egress subnet with tight route tables and egress-only rules.
[01:48] Evan: we have a strict policy - no outbound to public S3, only VPC endpoints allowed. any NAT hairpin or egress path has to be auditable.
[02:02] Samir: understood. one pattern we've used is dedicated isolated subnets for runtime nodes with no Internet gateway. then a separate managed egress subnet with NAT Gateway and a proxy that whitelists IPs for model fetch or telemetry. for PrivateLink specifically, you set up interface endpoints in your VPC and allow traffic to Redwood's private dns.
[02:27] Jared: there's the hairpin issue though — when nodes try to reach PrivateLink-bound endpoints in the same VPC, we saw packets leaving the subnet and failing source/destination checks. any tips?
[02:40] Lila: yeah, that's the classic source/dest check problem. you need to make sure the ENI for the PrivateLink acceptance is in the right AZ and the route tables point to the interface endpoint. if you're using NAT in the same subnet, disable source/dest check on the ENI and ensure the security groups allow the internal CIDR. sometimes Linux host routing also needs policy routing rules so return packets flow correctly.
[03:06] Priya: so is that something Redwood manages on the PrivateLink side, or we have to do infra changes?
[03:12] Samir: Redwood can provide the CloudFormation/Terraform templates that create the endpoint service and show the accept/attach steps. for PrivateLink the customer must accept and attach the interface endpoint; we can automate some of it via our onboarding script but infra changes are typically on the customer side.
[03:28] Jared: got it. moving into DNS — if we enable private DNS, what's the recommended resolver config? split-horizon?
[03:37] Lila: we recommend enabling private DNS for the interface endpoint so your calls to api.redwood.example (our example host) resolve to the interface IPs. for customers with split-horizon, point the VPC resolver to a centralized forwarding resolver — that way internal hostnames still resolve. beware TTLs and our SDK's connection pooling which caches IPs; if endpoint ENIs failover across AZs you might need to flush connections.
[04:03] Damien: small note — our runtime keeps persistent HTTP2 or GRPC connections to reduce cold-start token overhead. if DNS updates mid-stream, existing connections won't pick up new IPs, so we have keepalives and a periodic reconnect policy (default 10s graceful drain) but you can tune that.
[04:23] Evan: that reconnect window concerns us, because we have latency SLOs. if an AZ goes down, we don't want a 10s blackhole. can we shorten that?
[04:32] Lila: yes, we can lower the drain to 2–3s, but you trade off transient increased CPU while reconnecting. for strict SLOs we recommend multi-AZ clients + per-AZ endpoint binding and health checks in the routing policy.
[04:55] Jared: switching to KV cache — our inference workload is chat-like with long context. we rely on KV caching to avoid re-encoding prefix tokens. how do you keep KV cache coherent across nodes in different AZs?
[05:10] Damien: Redwood runtime uses local KV cache with optional remote invalidation messages. simplest pattern: pin requests to the same AZ (session affinity) so the hot KV cache stays warm. if you need cross-AZ resiliency we do a pub/sub invalidation via the control plane; you'll see a slightly higher tail latency on cold miss if the remote cache needs to fetch.
[05:31] Priya: session affinity sounds fine but our traffic is behind an internal load balancer that balances by round-robin. can we do sticky routing?
[05:40] Samir: yep we can set the LB to use least-conn or a cookie-based stickiness. another pattern: use a small shared redis/kv-store for frequently-mutated prefixes, but that adds network latency — usually 1–4ms extra.
[05:53] Jared: any recomms on TTL/eviction? we have variable prompt lengths, sometimes the prefix is huge.
[06:00] Lila: TTL should reflect typical conversation warm period; for chat apps, 30–90s is common before eviction, but memory pressure and KV slot count matter. we provide telemetry to show cache hit ratio and eviction churn so you can size nodes.
[06:12] Evan: are these KV caches encrypted at rest or in transit?
[06:16] Damien: in transit always TLS, at rest depends on deployment — for Redwood Private we integrate with customer KMS/HSM or managed volume encryption.
[06:24] Jared: batching — our P99 for token latency needs to be sub-200ms. how much batching can we do without blowing that SLA?
[06:33] Lila: batching is a knob. smaller batching windows (5–15ms) get you decent throughput benefit for short queries without adding too much tail. for strict tail latency we recommend adaptive batching: batch up to N tokens or T ms whichever triggers first. Redwood Optimize can suggest initial N and T based on your token distribution.
[06:55] Priya: what's the CPU/GC impact of very short windows? we've seen JVM-like runtimes thrash if the load is spiky.
[07:02] Damien: true for some runtimes — our engine is largely C++ with controlled memory allocs; still, very small windows increase scheduling overhead. there's a sweet spot at 10–30ms for most conversational workloads. we'll share benchmark graphs.
[07:18] Jared: quantization — Orion is considering int8 quantized models to reduce memory. how does quantization affect latency and batching?
[07:28] Lila: quantization reduces memory footprint so you can fit larger batches on the same GPU, improving throughput. however, quantized kernels sometimes change per-token latency slightly — especially for attention kernel reorderings. expect 5–15% improvement in throughput but tail latency variance may increase slightly. we recommend testing both int8 and int4 profiles.
[07:48] Samir: and note, quantization interacts with KV cache sizes — smaller checkpoints mean faster KV cache restore on cold start.
[07:57] Evan: what about warmup? if we spin new nodes in an AZ, how long to warm the KV and model artifacts?
[08:05] Damien: depends on model size. for a 13B model with quantized weights on NVMe local storage, artifact load is ~20–45s; KV warmup for chat prefixes depends on traffic — we often run synthetic warmers that ping typical prefixes to pre-populate the KV. we can provide a warmup script.
[08:23] Priya: can that warmup traffic be internal-only? we don't want warmed-up data going to telemetry collectors in Redwood.
[08:30] Samir: yes, that can be configured to stay internal. telemetry opt-out is possible for Private deployments; you can either forward metrics to your own collector or allow Redwood to collect anonymized telemetry only.
[08:45] Jared: security check — our InfoSec wants RBAC and audit logs for inference requests. is there request-level logging for who invoked what model?
[08:55] Lila: yes, we support token-level audit logs, request metadata, and can integrate with your SIEM. logs can be stored in your S3 bucket with server-side encryption and an optional redaction layer to avoid storing PHI content.
[09:09] Evan: about network policies: if we put nodes in isolated subnets, what NAT or egress rules are required for model rollouts?
[09:19] Damien: you only need outbound for artifact fetches, optional license verifications, and updates. those can be limited to specific IPs or VPC endpoints. our recommended pattern is a minimal egress host that proxies to allowed endpoints, combined with strict route tables and security group rules.
[09:34] Priya: are there any known issues when using an egress proxy + PrivateLink and DNS resolver forwarding?
[09:42] Lila: proxying can complicate TLS mutual-auth if the proxy rewrites SNI. make sure the proxy preserves SNI and does TCP passthrough for TLS connections unless you intend to terminate TLS at the proxy. for HTTP traffic we support mTLS to Redwood if required.
[09:58] Jared: we are worried about IP churn when we scale nodes up/down, will that break long-lived streams (websockets / streaming outputs)?
[10:08] Damien: long-lived streams are bound to an instance until you drain. our draining policy is graceful — we finish inflight streams and then shutdown, but if the node loses connectivity you'll transiently re-route to another instance and the client may need to reconnect. best practice: client-side reconnect logic with exponential backoff; also use session affinity to reduce mid-stream reassignment.
[10:30] Samir: quick architecture sketch — three subnet tiers: management (api plane for control), runtime (isolated nodes), egress (NAT + proxy). PrivateLink interface endpoints bound into management subnet for control-plane calls. runtime nodes talk to management plane over internal-only paths.
[10:50] Priya: does Redwood require specific MTU settings? we have jumbo MTU and sometimes packet fragmentation messes up GRPC streams.
[10:58] Lila: we recommend standard 1500 MTU on the data plane unless you have tuned your infra. jumbo frames are ok but ensure all hops support it; otherwise you'll get path MTU issues. also watch for AWS ENI limits per instance when you have many network interfaces for PrivateLink.
[11:16] Jared: any guidance on monitoring — how to correlate network-level drops with KV cache misses and inference error rates?
[11:25] Damien: our console exposes per-route latencies, cache hit ratios, and pod-level health. we also ship tracing hooks that emit spans for cache hit/miss, batching windows and egress time. you can send traces to your Jaeger/Zipkin or to our console. correlating via trace IDs makes debugging easy.
[11:43] Evan: we need the SOC2 artifact and any penetration tests for your private deployment package.
[11:50] Samir: we'll attach our SOC2 packaging and the penetration test summary. for Private deployments we also provide an architecture security checklist.
[11:58] Priya: last thing — can we do a quick experiment: mid-call run a tiny benchmark that simulates 200rps, 8 tokens avg, session-affinity vs no affinity, to see cache hit ratio?
[12:09] Lila: we can show a sample script but we shouldn't run heavy loads on your prod account. we can set it up in your staging VPC and run tomorrow.
[12:18] Jared: that works. can Redwood also provide a target config for batch window and KV sizes to start with?
[12:24] Damien: yes, we'll include a suggested config as part of the onboarding bundle — it's what we normally give to other healthcare customers.
[12:31] Samir: ok recap of action items — Samir: share network diagram and security pack; Lila: share warmup script and batching experiment; Jared: provision staging VPC and accept PrivateLink; set meeting to run benchmark next week.
[12:48] Jared: thanks everyone. anything else?
[12:50] Evan: one tiny note — encryption key lifecycle: we want rotation capability without service disruption.
[12:56] Damien: supported — we rotate keys with rolling restarts and you can bring-your-own-KMS. we'll share the rotation playbook.
[13:06] Samir: great, we'll follow up with docs and the templates. thanks all.

End of transcript.
